newsitem.title: UK: British tycoon makes big donation to Labour.
newsitem.headline: British tycoon makes big donation to Labour.

text.p: A soccer-loving entrepreneur has pledged one million pounds ($1.57 million) to Britain's Labour Party, giving a major boost to opposition finances just months before an election.

Matthew Harding, reported to be Britain's 87th richest person, dealt another blow to Prime Minister John Major with a ringing endorsement of Labour's Tony Blair, whom he called in a statement "the best leader for our country".

The gift -- the largest amount of cash donated to the Labour Party by an individual in its 90-year history -- crowns a week in which Blair has wooed businessmen and tried to embarrass the ruling Conservatives by unveiling the opposition's major donors.

The Conservatives, struggling to cover large debts as corporate sponsors have melted away, refuse to name donors. Labour accuses the ruling party of accepting funds from questionable sources, some of them located abroad.
Labour, which Blair has dragged into the political centre since taking over as leader in 1994, bans overseas donations.

An added twist to Friday's news is that insurance company boss Harding is vice-chairman of Chelsea football club, Major's favourite team. Harding and the prime minister have met frequently in the VIP box at the Chelsea ground.

Newspapers said on Friday Harding had been advising Labour, sitting on a huge opinion poll lead of between 20 and 30 points ahead of an election due by mid-1997, on how to raise funds and win over businessmen.

In his statement, Harding said: "I want to help Tony and the Labour Party to bring about change in this country. As Tony said yesterday, it is unhealthy for our political life when one party is supported by business and the other not."

At a conference of top businessmen on Wednesday hosted by Labour, Blair was hailed for his success in developing new business-friendly policies. In an announcement timed to coincide with the conference, Cob Stenham, the chairman of Anglo-French packaging group Arjo Wiggins, became the first head of a top listed company publicly to back Blair.
Labour announced this week it received 17 donations of more than 5,000 pounds last year.
Many were from unions but a handful were from wealthy individuals, including publisher Paul Hamlyn and Philip Jeffrey, the multi-millionaire founder of a home improvement chain.
Boosted further by thousands of new recruits attracted by Blair's modernising image, Labour's campaign "war chest" reached 4.4 million pounds at the end of last year.

By May next year, the last date for an election, Labour expects to have more than doubled this. The Conservatives, meanwhile, have been battling to pay off a 15.4 million pound overdraft mainly left over from their victorious 1992 election campaign.
Last week, the party announced that a surge in donations had allowed it to pay off all these debts.
But analysts say the party has only managed this by taking interest-free loans totalling over eight million pounds from local party associations, companies and rich supporters.
Corporate sponsors -- worried at Labour's poll lead and under pressure from shareholders to maximise profits -- have been closing their cheque books.

Key backers like Lucas Industries, the engineering group, car distributor Inchcape, drinks group Allied Domecq, British Airways and even United Biscuits, for many years the party's biggest supporter, have stopped donations. ($1=.6373 Pound)
